clinicalPearls: A spectrum of abnormal development of the hip ranging from mild acetabular dysplasia to frank dislocation, present at or developing after birth.
Major risk factors include female sex, breech presentation, oligohydramnios, first-born status, and a positive family history.
Newborn screening uses the Barlow manoeuvre (to dislocate a reducible hip) and the Ortolani manoeuvre (to relocate a dislocated hip).
In older infants, signs include limited hip abduction, asymmetric thigh or gluteal skin creases, and apparent limb-length discrepancy (Galeazzi sign).
Ultrasound is the imaging test of choice in early infancy before the femoral head ossifies; plain radiographs become useful after a few months of age.
Early treatment of a reducible hip with an abduction device such as the Pavlik harness is usually successful and avoids surgery.
The later the diagnosis, the more likely that closed or open reduction and casting, or surgical procedures, will be needed.
Untreated or late-treated dysplasia leads to a limp, gait abnormality, and premature degenerative hip arthritis in adulthood.
Persistent clicks alone are usually benign, whereas a palpable 'clunk' of dislocation or relocation is significant.
reference.pathophysiology: Laxity of the hip capsule and abnormal relationship between the femoral head and acetabulum, influenced by maternal hormones, intrauterine packing (as in breech position and oligohydramnios), and genetic factors, allow the femoral head to sit incompletely within or outside a shallow acetabulum. Without a well-seated femoral head, the acetabulum fails to develop its normal depth and shape, perpetuating instability and, over time, leading to secondary degenerative change.
additionalDifferentials: Neuromuscular hip dysplasia (e.g. in cerebral palsy or spina bifida)
Proximal focal femoral deficiency or other congenital femoral anomalies
additionalInvestigations: Hip ultrasound in the first months of life
Anteroposterior pelvic radiograph after the femoral head ossifies
Careful serial clinical examination including Barlow, Ortolani, and Galeazzi tests
Targeted imaging for high-risk infants (breech, family history)
redFlags: A frankly dislocated or non-reducible hip on examination
Delayed diagnosis presenting as a limp or abnormal gait in a walking child
Bilateral dislocation, which can be harder to detect due to symmetry
Failure of a hip to stabilise despite bracing
reference.prognosis: When detected and treated in early infancy, most hips develop normally with excellent long-term function; delayed diagnosis increases the need for surgery and the risk of residual dysplasia, avascular necrosis, and early osteoarthritis.
pitfalls: Missing dysplasia in bilateral cases where symmetry masks the abnormality
Over-relying on benign hip clicks or reassurance from a single normal newborn examination
Not imaging or closely following high-risk infants (breech, family history) with a normal exam
Applying an abduction device too tightly, risking femoral head avascular necrosis
Failing to recognise late-presenting DDH in a child with a limp or waddling gait
